Population Structure Overview

This table summarises the key typing results for each genome. Understanding the population structure helps identify dominant clones, track outbreaks, and link genotypes to phenotypes.

  • MLST (Sequence Type): Gold standard for global epidemiology. Clonal complexes indicate recent common ancestry.
  • Serotype (O:H): Surface antigens used for traditional typing. Specific O:H combinations are associated with pathotypes (e.g., O157:H7 with STEC).
  • Phylogroup (Clermont): Deep evolutionary lineages (A, B1, B2, C, D, E, F, G). Phylogroup B2 and D are often extra-intestinal pathogenic (ExPEC), while A and B1 are commensal/environmental.
  • CH Type (FumC:FimH): Fine‑scale typing based on housekeeping (FumC) and adhesin (FimH) genes. FimH alleles correlate with tropism and virulence.
  • Pathotype: Predicted diarrheagenic or extra‑intestinal pathotype based on VFDB genes.

MLST Analysis

Multi‑Locus Sequence Typing (MLST) uses internal fragments of seven housekeeping genes. It is highly reproducible and defines Sequence Types (STs). Closely related STs belong to the same Clonal Complex (CC).

11 unique STs identified. MLST is the gold standard for global epidemiology and outbreak tracking.

Pathotype Classification & Prevalence

E. coli pathotypes are defined by specific combinations of virulence factors. This section shows the prevalence of each pathotype in your dataset and allows you to explore which samples belong to which category.

Pathotype definitions based on VFDB. Credit: Kevin Blake, PhD (PathotypeR).

Pathotype definitions:

  • STEC (Shiga toxin-producing E. coli): stx1/stx2, eae absent → causes haemorrhagic colitis and HUS.
  • EPEC (Enteropathogenic E. coli): eae/bfpA, no stx → infant diarrhoea.
  • EHEC (Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli): stx + eae → severe bloody diarrhoea, HUS.
  • EAEC (Enteroaggregative E. coli): aggR/aaiC/aatA → persistent diarrhoea.
  • ETEC (Enterotoxigenic E. coli): lt/sta → traveller's diarrhoea.
  • DAEC (Diffusely adherent E. coli): afaC/afaE → diarrhoea in children.
  • EIEC (Enteroinvasive E. coli): ipaH → dysentery-like illness.
  • none: No markers for the above pathotypes.

Surveillance importance: Knowing which pathotypes circulate helps guide clinical management, vaccine development, and outbreak response. STEC/EHEC are particularly important for food safety.

AMR Gene Analysis (Gene‑Centric)

Each AMR gene is shown with all genomes that carry it. Use filter buttons to focus on important resistance classes. The genome search box highlights specific isolates across the table – useful for tracking which samples carry a particular gene combination.

Surveillance importance: Tracking ESBL, carbapenemase, and colistin resistance genes is crucial for antimicrobial stewardship and outbreak detection. Critical resistance genes are marked with ⚠️.

Key AMR Gene Classes & Their Clinical Importance
  • ESBLs (blaCTX‑M, blaSHV, blaTEM) – Break down extended‑spectrum cephalosporins; limit treatment options.
  • Carbapenemases (blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA, blaVIM, blaIMP) – Destroy carbapenems (last‑line antibiotics); WHO critical priority.
  • Colistin resistance (mcr, pmr, lpx, arn) – Threatens last‑resort drug for MDR infections; plasmid‑mediated spread.
  • Quinolone resistance (qnr, gyrA, parC) – Reduces fluoroquinolone efficacy; often combined with other mechanisms.
  • Aminoglycoside resistance (aac, aph, ant, armA) – Common in hospital isolates; armA causes high‑level resistance.
  • Tetracycline (tet) – Efflux or ribosomal protection; widespread in commensals and pathogens.
  • Sulfonamide/Trimethoprim (sul, dfr) – Resistance to common oral agents; often carried on integrons.
  • Phenicol (cat, floR) – Resistance to chloramphenicol and florfenicol; veterinary importance.
  • Macrolide (erm, mph, msr) – Increasingly reported in Enterobacteriaceae; link to azithromycin failure.
  • Hover over any gene name in the table for more details.

Virulence Gene Analysis (Gene‑Centric)

Each virulence gene is shown with all genomes that carry it. Use filter buttons to focus on key pathotype determinants. The genome search box highlights specific isolates.

Surveillance importance: Virulence profiles differentiate harmless commensals from pathogenic strains. Shiga toxins (stx), intimin (eae), and other markers are critical for public health risk assessment. Critical virulence genes are marked with ⚠️.

Key Virulence Genes & Their Roles
  • stx1/stx2 – Shiga toxins: cause haemorrhagic colitis and HUS (STEC/EHEC).
  • eae – Intimin: intimate attachment, essential for EPEC/EHEC.
  • bfpA – Bundle‑forming pilus: adherence in EPEC.
  • aggR – Master regulator of EAEC virulence (aggregative adherence, toxins).
  • lt/sta1 – Heat‑labile/‑stable toxins: cause watery diarrhoea (ETEC).
  • ipaH – Invasion plasmid antigen: cell invasion (EIEC/Shigella).
  • cnf1 – Cytotoxic necrotising factor: cytoskeletal changes (ExPEC).
  • hlyA – α‑hemolysin: pore‑forming toxin (UPEC).
  • kps – Capsule: immune evasion (ExPEC).
  • iuc – Aerobactin: iron acquisition (ExPEC/EAEC).
  • Hover over any gene name in the table for more details.

Plasmid Replicons & Serotyping (PlasmidFinder + EcoH)

This table combines two important analyses:

  • PlasmidFinder: Identifies plasmid replicon markers (e.g., IncF, IncI, Col), which are vehicles for horizontal gene transfer of AMR and virulence genes.
  • EcoH: Predicts O and H antigens for E. coli serotyping (e.g., O157:H7). Serotypes are crucial for outbreak surveillance and pathotype identification.

Use the genome search box to highlight specific isolates. Tracking epidemic plasmids and serotypes helps understand the spread of resistance and pathogenic clones.

Bacmet2 Database: Biocide, Heavy Metal & Stress Resistance

These genes confer resistance to disinfectants (quaternary ammonium, chlorhexidine, formaldehyde), heavy metals (mercury, arsenic, copper, silver, chromium, cadmium, zinc, lead), and stress responses that can co‑select with antibiotic resistance.

Surveillance importance: Tracking biocide resistance helps evaluate infection control measures. Metal resistance markers indicate potential co‑selection with AMR genes in hospital and agricultural environments.

Key Bacmet Categories & Their Roles
  • Biocides (qac, cep, form) – Resistance to disinfectants and antiseptics used in hospitals. Their spread could compromise infection control.
  • Heavy metals (mer, ars, cop, sil, chr, cad, znt, czc, pbr) – Resistance to mercury, arsenic, copper, silver, chromium, cadmium, zinc, cobalt, lead. Often co‑located with AMR genes on plasmids and integrons.
  • Stress regulators (soxR, cpxR, baeR) – Activate efflux pumps and stress responses, indirectly contributing to multidrug resistance.
  • Efflux pumps (ade, mex, emr, sme, norA) – Export not only antibiotics but also biocides, heavy metals, and dyes. Major players in co‑selection.
  • Hover over any gene name in the table for more details.

🤖 AI Assistant Guide – Your Co‑Pilot for Science, Not a Substitute

You’ve generated a rich dataset. Now let AI help you turn numbers into narratives – ethically, responsibly, and with you in the driver’s seat.

The Golden Rule of AI in Science:
AI is like a hyper‑caffeinated grad student who never sleeps – great at summarising, spotting patterns, and drafting, but it can hallucinate, cite fake papers, and misunderstand context. Always verify, always think critically, and never let AI replace your expert judgment. 😉

🚀 How to Use This Report with AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.)

  1. Export the full data as JSON but I'd prefer this HTML (click the Export tab → "Download JSON").
  2. Upload the JSON file to your preferred AI chat interface (e.g., ChatGPT Plus with file upload, Claude, or Gemini Advanced).
  3. Ask specific, contextual questions – the AI will read your actual data and answer based on it.
  4. Use the generated insights to draft sections of your manuscript, thesis, or public health report – but always fact‑check against the original tables.

📝 Using AI to Draft Manuscripts & Theses – A Step‑by‑Step Workflow

Scenario: You've analysed 200 E. coli genomes and want to write a paper on "Genomic epidemiology of ESBL‑producing E. coli in Ghana".

Step 1 – Let AI generate an outline:
"Based on the JSON data, suggest a logical structure for a scientific paper covering: population structure (MLST, serotypes), AMR gene prevalence, pathotype distribution, and high‑risk combinations."

Step 2 – Draft the Methods section:
"Write a methods paragraph describing how we used AMRFinderPlus, ABRicate (VFDB, PlasmidFinder, EcoH, Bacmet2), and the custom GENIUS pipeline to classify pathotypes."

Step 3 – Summarise key results in plain English:
"From the JSON, what are the top 5 most common AMR genes and their percentages? Format as bullet points."

Step 4 – Generate a draft discussion:
"Based on the prevalence of blaCTX‑M (45%), mcr-1 (3%), and the identification of ST131 (30% of isolates), draft a discussion paragraph on the public health implications."

Step 5 – Polish and cross‑reference:
Ask AI to rephrase, shorten, or expand specific sentences, but manually verify every number and citation.

🎓 For Thesis Writers – Let AI Be Your Writing Coach

  • Generate figure/table captions: "Write a descriptive caption for the pathotype prevalence table (STEC 20%, EPEC 15%, …)."
  • Rewrite passive voice to active: "Change this sentence to active voice: 'The blaCTX-M gene was detected in 45% of isolates.'"
  • Create a graphical abstract concept: "Describe a graphical abstract that visualises the main findings: ST131 dominance, high ESBL rate, and presence of mcr-1."
  • Summarise limitations: "Based on the QC metrics (e.g., N50 values), what limitations should I mention in the discussion?"

⚠️ Ethical Guardrails – Because With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility

  • ❌ Never paste unreviewed AI output directly into a manuscript – treat it as a first draft, not a final product.
  • ✅ Always cite the AI tool if you use verbatim text (check journal policies – many now require disclosure).
  • 🔍 Fact‑check every number, gene name, and reference – AI can invent plausible‑sounding nonsense (confabulation).
  • 👥 Keep human experts in the loop – AI is a co‑pilot, not the captain. Your thesis advisor, co‑authors, and reviewers are irreplaceable.
  • 🌍 Use AI to democratise science – non‑native English speakers can use it to improve clarity, but always acknowledge its use.

Humour break: AI once told a colleague that "the plasmid IncF was discovered by Galileo in 1610". Don't be that person. Verify, verify, verify!

Our Philosophy: We are in the era of AI‑augmented science. Used ethically, AI can accelerate public health research, reduce language barriers, and empower researchers in low‑resource settings. But it must never replace human curiosity, critical thinking, or domain expertise. You are the expert – AI is your enthusiastic, occasionally forgetful assistant. 🧠🤝🤖

The Global Burden of AMR and Our Call to Action

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the top global public health threats, with an estimated 1.27 million direct deaths annually. Escherichia coli is a major contributor, causing urinary tract infections, bloodstream infections, and foodborne outbreaks. Tracking AMR and virulence determinants is essential to inform treatment guidelines and infection control.

We developed ECOLITYPER to empower researchers and clinicians – especially in low‑resource settings – to analyse their own sequencing data without extensive bioinformatics expertise.

ESCAPE AMR – Our Ongoing Project (ESKAPE Pathogens)

ECOLITYPER is one of the first module of a larger initiative called ESCAPE AMR (formerly ESKAPE). We target the notorious ESKAPE pathogens:

  • Enterococcus faecium
  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Acinetobacter baumannii
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Enterobacter species (including E. coli)

These bacteria “escape” the effects of antibiotics – hence the name. But we believe the name is also a global call to action:

🔹 Everyone must join forces – researchers, clinicians, policymakers, and citizens.
🔹 Smart surveillance is our first line of defence. No more guessing – we need genomic data.
🔹 Knowledge must be shared openly. No paywalls, no closed silos.
🔹 Africa bears a heavy AMR burden, but African solutions are already emerging.
🔹 Prevention is cheaper than cure. Let's stop resistant infections before they spread.
🔹 Every day we delay, more lives are at stake. The time to act is now, not tomorrow.

“We didn’t choose the name ESKAPE because it sounds cool (though it does). We chose it because it reminds us every single day: we must ESCAPE the AMR crisis – together, urgently, and with the best science we have.”
— Brown Beckley, lead developer (who secretly hopes this pun makes you smile, not roll your eyes 😉)
